title: Open-ended, closed-ended and interval funds; how NAV works
objectives: Tell open-ended, closed-ended and interval schemes apart.
Calculate a NAV from a simple balance sheet.
Explain why a low NAV does not mean a cheap fund.
body_md:
## Three structures

| Type | How you buy and sell | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Open-ended | Any business day, directly from the AMC at NAV, with no fixed maturity | Most schemes, including SIPs |
| Closed-ended | Only in the NFO, then on the stock exchange at market price, until a fixed maturity | Fixed-term products; the market price can differ from NAV |
| Interval | Open for purchase and redemption only at specified intervals | Short-term parking where liquidity is planned |

<!-- TODO-VERIFY: ELSS and some solution-oriented schemes are close-ended or lock-in schemes; check the current SEBI category rules before stating exceptions. -->

## What NAV is

**NAV (Net Asset Value)** is the value of one unit. The AMC calculates it every business day after markets close:

NAV = (market value of all investments + cash and receivables, less liabilities and expenses) ÷ units outstanding

A scheme's NAV tells you what one unit costs today. It does **not** tell you whether the fund is cheap or expensive. A fund with a NAV of ₹10 and a fund with a NAV of ₹200 can both deliver the same percentage return.

## Why units move

When the market value of the portfolio rises, the NAV rises. Dividends (IDCW) paid out reduce the NAV by the amount paid, so a payout is not extra return.

> **Investor takeaway:** Judge a fund on its returns, risk and cost, never on the size of its NAV.
example: A scheme holds investments worth ₹500 crore and ₹10 crore of cash and receivables. Its liabilities and expenses are ₹5 crore, and 50 crore units are outstanding. NAV = (500 + 10 − 5) ÷ 50 = ₹10.10 per unit.
say: NAV is just the price of one unit today. It does not tell you if a fund is cheap.
An open-ended fund lets you buy or sell on any business day at that day's NAV.
never: This fund is only ₹12, so it is cheaper than that ₹250 one.
A closed-ended fund is just like an open-ended fund.

check.q: A fund has a NAV of ₹12 and another has a NAV of ₹250. What can you say?
o: The ₹12 fund is cheaper and better value
NAV level alone says nothing about value or future returns
check.why: NAV is the price of one unit. Returns depend on the portfolio, not the unit price.

check.q: Which scheme type can be bought and redeemed on any business day at NAV?
check.why: Open-ended schemes allow purchase and redemption on any business day at the applicable NAV.

check.q: A scheme has assets of ₹210, cash of ₹10, and liabilities of ₹20. With 20 units outstanding, what is the NAV?
